sections.h2: Selling a house in Upper Darby
sections.html:
Upper Darby is a dense, close-in Delaware County township just west of Philadelphia. It is a first-class township of more than 85,000 residents packed into 7.9 square miles, and the 2020 census counted 85,681 people. Most of the housing is older and built close together: row houses and twins along streets like Richfield Road, a legacy of the building boom that followed the 1907 extension of the Market-Frankford elevated line to 69th Street.

Neighborhood names matter when you price a home. Drexel Hill, Secane, Primos, Bywood, Beverly Hills, Aronimink, Highland Park and Stonehurst each draw a different kind of buyer. Transit is the strongest selling point most owners have: the 69th Street Transportation Center at Terminal Square is the end of the Market-Frankford Line and the start of the Norristown High Speed Line, with trolley routes 101 and 102 and many bus lines.

  • Time the walk to the El or a trolley stop before you write the listing.
  • Name the school zone in your description only after the school district confirms it.
  • Mention off-street parking if you have it. On rowhouse blocks it is scarce.

Settlement cannot happen without a Use and Occupancy (U&O) certificate. The township applies it to every sale and transfer, and the seller is the one who has to obtain it.

The application has to reach the Licenses & Inspections office at least 14 business days before settlement, and the township suggests four weeks because of demand. An inspector then calls to set a visit. Inspectors look without opening walls, measuring the house against the property maintenance code and township ordinances. There are three possible results:

  • Final certificate: the house is compliant and can be occupied.
  • Temporary certificate: minor violations exist, and the buyer must correct them within one year of purchase.
  • Temporary access certificate: substantial violations exist. Current occupants may stay, but no new occupant may move in.

Substantial violations include missing or dead smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, absent fire extinguishers where required, structural or electrical hazards, and an unfiled sewer lateral certification. The sewer lateral certification has to come from an approved Upper Darby contractor. When the buyer agrees to handle repairs, a notarized Letter of Intent must be filed. If the buyer named on the application changes, a new application, new fees and a new inspection follow. Payment is by L&I online payment, check or money order. Cash is refused. Call 610-734-7613 to check the current fee schedule.

sections.h2: Taxes and fees that come out of a sale
sections.html:
Realty transfer tax is the big one. The state's 1 percent is collected along with a local tax by the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds. Most Delaware County municipalities charge 1 percent locally, but Upper Darby moved to 1.5 percent on January 1, 2022, for a combined 2.5 percent. The state holds buyer and seller jointly responsible, which makes the contract the place to assign the cost.

The Recorder's office is in Room 108 of the Government Center at 201 W. Front Street in Media, with recording hours of 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

sections.h2: Property tax bills and unpaid balances
sections.html:
Three separate bills arrive, and the township collects only its own. The Upper Darby Tax Office bills real estate tax, a sewer charge and a trash fee. School tax goes to the Upper Darby School District Tax Office (610-789-7200, extension 3210), and county tax goes to the Delaware County Property Tax Office (610-891-4278).

On the township bill, real estate tax earns a 2 percent discount if paid before April 1, then carries face value through May 31 and a 10 percent penalty after that. Sewer and trash bills skip the discount: face value by May 31, then the same penalty. Anything unpaid after December 31 goes to an outside collection agency, and the township stops taking payment. A delinquent amount is a lien against the parcel, so expect the title company to find it and ask for payoff at settlement.

A tax certification tells a buyer's side exactly what is owed. Standard requests take five to seven business days and come back by mail or FedEx, so order one early if you are on a tight closing schedule.

sections.h2: Can I appeal my assessment before I sell?
sections.html:
Yes. The county, and not the township, hears assessment appeals. Forms are posted on the county's Board of Assessment page, with separate versions for residential, commercial and exemption appeals. Completed forms go to the Government Center Building in Media. Fax and electronic filings are refused, and each form must carry an original signature.

Because mail postmarks can slip, the county urges filers to walk the form in to the Media office. The other safe routes start at a post office counter: a manual postmark, a certificate of mailing, certified or registered delivery, or postage bought over the counter. If the Board rules against you, a court appeal has to start within 30 days of its findings, through the Office of Judicial Support.

The assessment office also handles homestead questions, and it can tell you the filing deadline for your tax year.

sections.h2: Should I list, repair or take a cash offer?
sections.html:
Condition and timing decide which route fits. A listing can bring the best price on a sound home in Drexel Hill or Secane, but it carries agent fees, showings and a U&O inspection. A cash buyer can often close without waiting on financing, though the sale still needs the U&O certificate and the sewer lateral paperwork.

  • A listing suits a house in good repair when you can wait out several weeks.
  • Fix the substantial violations first if you want a final certificate, because smoke and CO detectors are cheap to correct.
  • Sell as-is for cash if repairs, tenants or an inherited property make the timeline hard, and let the buyer take on the temporary certificate work.
  • If the home is a rental, the township requires a rental license application for non-owner-occupied properties.

Before signing anything, get the offer in writing, decide who covers the 2.5 percent transfer tax, and check that the U&O schedule fits the closing date.

faqs.q: How long does the Upper Darby use and occupancy process take?
faqs.a: Plan on four weeks. The township requires the application at least 14 business days before settlement and recommends four weeks because inspections are in demand. If the buyer on the application changes, a new application and a fresh inspection are required.

faqs.q: Who pays the Upper Darby transfer tax?
faqs.a: Both sides are liable to the state, so the contract settles who actually pays. The total is 2.5 percent: 1 percent to the Commonwealth plus Upper Darby's 1.5 percent.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Upper Darby with code violations?
faqs.a: Yes, in many cases. Minor violations lead to a temporary certificate and the buyer has one year to fix them. Substantial violations lead to a temporary access certificate, which lets current occupants stay but bars new occupants until the work is done.

faqs.q: Does a landlord need a rental license before selling in Upper Darby?
faqs.a: Yes, a rental license application belongs in the U&O packet for any property that is not owner-occupied. Ask Licenses & Inspections whether your license is current before you list.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed after an Upper Darby closing?
faqs.a: In Media, in Room 108 of the county Government Center, where transfer tax is collected with the deed. The recording desk takes documents from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and whoever handles your settlement usually files for you.
